articles.title: DH Shipbuilding reports strong nine-month profit growth
articles.summary: South Korea’s DH Shipbuilding reported strong financial results for the first nine months of 2026, supported by higher-value vessel construction and improved shipyard productivity. The shipbuilder recorded cumulative revenue of KRW 990.4 billion and operating profit of KRW 260.6 billion through September, achieving...
articles.body: South Korea’s DH Shipbuilding reported strong financial results for the first nine months of 2026, supported by higher-value vessel construction and improved shipyard productivity. The shipbuilder recorded cumulative revenue of KRW 990.4 billion and operating profit of KRW 260.6 billion through September, achieving an operating profit margin of 26.3%. For the third quarter alone, revenue reached KRW 327.7 billion, while operating profit stood at KRW 82.7 billion. The company attributed its earnings performance to the construction of higher-priced vessels ordered in 2024, alongside productivity improvements from building established vessel designs. DH Shipbuilding has maintained an operating profit margin above 20% for eight consecutive quarters. Margins have also remained above 25% for the last four consecutive quarters. Shipbuilding backlog supports future operations DH Shipbuilding continued to secure new vessel orders during 2026, particularly in the crude oil tanker segment. The company has received orders for 17 Suezmax tankers worth approximately US$1.5 billion this year, exceeding its annual order target by 62%. As of 30 September 2026, its order backlog stood at 35 vessels with a combined value of approximately US$3.3 billion. The existing orderbook provides the shipbuilder with contracted work for the coming years, although the announcement does not specify the delivery schedule for individual vessels. DH Shipbuilding’s nine-month operating profit was equivalent to approximately 89% of the KRW 294.1 billion recorded for the full year of 2025. The company could therefore exceed last year’s annual operating profit if its recent earnings performance continues during the final quarter. However, this remains dependent on the company’s fourth-quarter operating results. New shareholder return policy announced Alongside its earnings update, DH Shipbuilding announced a medium-term shareholder return policy covering the period from 2027 to 2029. Under the plan, the company intends to return at least 30% of its annual consolidated net income to shareholders through cash dividends, share repurchases and share cancellations. The shipbuilder has also approved an additional KRW 10 billion share buyback. Further decisions on dividends, repurchases and cancellations will follow the completion of its financial statements. According to the company, the policy is intended to distribute a portion of future earnings to shareholders while supporting long-term corporate value. The latest results highlight DH Shipbuilding’s continued profitability, supported by its existing vessel backlog and production efficiency improvements.
takeaways: South Korea’s DH Shipbuilding reported strong financial results for the first nine months of 2026, supported by higher-value vessel construction and improved shipyard productivity.
The shipbuilder recorded cumulative revenue of KRW 990.4 billion and operating profit of KRW 260.6 billion through September, achieving an operating profit margin of 26.3%.
For the third quarter alone, revenue reached KRW 327.7 billion, while operating profit stood at KRW 82.7 billion.

articles.body: Mitsui O.S.K. Lines (MOL) reported a sharp increase in containership earnings during the first half of its 2026 fiscal year, supported by stronger profitability at Ocean Network Express (ONE), elevated freight rates and continued capacity constraints across major container shipping routes. The Japanese shipping group’s containership business generated ordinary profit of ¥73.4 billion for the six months ended 30 September 2026, compared with ¥23.9 billion in the corresponding period last year, representing an increase of 206.2%. Revenue from the segment rose 23.4% to ¥54.3 billion, while MOL recorded ¥64.1 billion in equity-method earnings from ONE, reflecting the carrier’s improved financial performance. Strong container market supports earnings According to MOL, container spot freight rates remained elevated, particularly on Asia-North America routes, where sustained cargo demand and congestion at major Asian ports continued to restrict effective vessel capacity. The company said ONE achieved a significant year-on-year improvement in profitability despite higher bunker fuel costs and the suspension of vessel deployments to the Persian Gulf. The stronger performance of its container shipping investment contributed to an increase in MOL’s overall earnings, alongside improvements in dry bulk and energy transportation. However, domestic container terminal operations experienced weaker handling volumes as vessel schedule disruptions caused by congestion at overseas ports affected operations. Meanwhile, MOL reported firm throughput at its overseas container terminal operations, supported by increased import and export activity in Vietnam, partly associated with the relocation of supply chains amid US-China trade tensions. Group profit rises despite higher operating costs MOL recorded consolidated revenue of ¥1.275 trillion during the first half of FY2026, representing a 46.6% increase from ¥869.8 billion a year earlier. Profit attributable to owners of the parent increased 54.3% to ¥179.3 billion, while ordinary profit rose 42.8% to ¥163.6 billion. Operating profit increased more modestly, rising 1.2% to ¥72.7 billion. The year-on-year comparison was affected by changes in the accounting periods of 384 consolidated subsidiaries, which resulted in nine months of their financial results being included in the current reporting period. For the containership segment specifically, the accounting adjustment increased reported revenue by approximately ¥8.8 billion and segment profit by ¥437 million. The company also faced substantially higher fuel costs, with average bunker prices increasing to US$865 per metric tonne from US$546 in the corresponding period last year. MOL maintains full-year earnings outlook MOL maintained its full-year financial forecast announced on 2 November, projecting consolidated revenue of ¥2.37 trillion and profit attributable to owners of the parent of ¥300 billion for the fiscal year ending 31 March 2027. The company expects its containership business to benefit from continued strong cargo demand and elevated freight rates, although higher fuel costs remain a significant challenge. Its financial outlook assumes that navigation in both the Persian Gulf and the Red Sea will remain unavailable throughout the fiscal year. MOL also expects domestic container terminal volumes to remain under pressure from vessel schedule disruptions, while overseas terminal operations are anticipated to maintain relatively firm handling volumes.
takeaways: Revenue from the segment rose 23.4% to ¥54.3 billion, while MOL recorded ¥64.1 billion in equity-method earnings from ONE, reflecting the carrier’s improved financial performance.
The company said ONE achieved a significant year-on-year improvement in profitability despite higher bunker fuel costs and the suspension of vessel deployments to the Persian Gulf.

articles.summary: The US Treasury Department may allow companies to buy sanctioned shipping vessels and return them to legitimate shipping on a case-by-case basis, according to a government source and a person with knowledge of the matter. “Treasury may consider proposals from legitimate shipping actors to purchase and restore shadow...
articles.body: US Treasury may allow purchase of sanctioned tankers on case basis in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 The US Treasury Department may allow companies to buy sanctioned shipping vessels and return them to legitimate shipping on a case-by-case basis, according to a government source and a person with knowledge of the matter. “Treasury may consider proposals from legitimate shipping actors to purchase and restore shadow fleet vessels to the licit shipping industry on a case-by-case basis,” a US official told Platts, part of S&P Global Energy. This approach “ensures that no sanctioned person receives any benefit, and reduces the size of the fleet overall, while helping address pressures on the global energy market,” the US official said. Another source with knowledge of the matter said Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control could be targeting 50-80 sanctioned tankers owned by non-sanctioned companies. There could be 20-30 owners willing to move quickly, the source said. At the end of September, there were a total of 1,225 tankers sanctioned by the US, UK or EU, S&P Global Commodities at Sea(opens in a new tab) said in an Oct. 29 shadow tanker report. Of those, 560 were sanctioned by the US. Shadow tankers are increasingly being drawn into the compliant market due to rising freight rates, according to a separate CAS market impact report issued Oct. 23. In 2026, 41 shadow-fleet crude tankers entered compliant trade through Oct. 20, with 68% remaining fully compliant so far, compared with just 17.5% of vessels that remained compliant in 2025. The shift to continued compliance was particularly notable in the third quarter when mainstream tanker earnings surged, the report said. Dirty Arab Gulf-China VLCC freight averaged approximately $197/mt in September, up 77% from August, the report said. CAS defines the shadow fleet as tankers that have transported Iranian or Russian oil in the last two years, vessels subject to US sanctions, and vessels with unknown or suspected false flag registrations. articles.body: Demand Rising in the Ship Recycling Markets in Hellenic Shipping News 12/11/2026 T he ship recycling market has been seeing increased demand for ships. In its latest weekly report, Best Oasis ( www.best-oasis.com ), a leading cash buyer of ships, said that “the Indian ship recycling market remains firm during the week, with buyers showing strong interest in acquiring suitable vessels for recycling. Local steel markets have softened, although the decline in the USD/INR exchange rate has provided some support to buying sentiment. A sanctioned LPG carrier was reportedly sold for recycling into India during the week, with no other sales reported. Overall, market sentiment remains firm, supported by sustained buying interest and continued demand for suitable recycling tonnage. The Bangladeshi ship recycling market continues to remain firm, with buyers actively seeking suitable vessels for recycling. Buying interest remains steady, with prevailing price indications largely unchanged from the previous week. Overall, market sentiment remains positive, supported by firm buying interest and stable pricing levels”. Best Oasis added that “the Pakistani ship recycling market remained largely unchanged this week, with subdued buying interest amid sluggish domestic market conditions. Continued pressure from Iranian imports, including unofficial cross-border trade, has further dampened breakers’ appetite for acquiring vessels. Vessel price indications remain broadly in line with the previous week, while market sentiment continues to range from moderate to subdued, with limited buying activity amid persistent pressure on domestic markets. Finally, the Turkish ship recycling market remains cautious, with limited vessel availability and weak purchasing activity. No new recycling sales were reported during the week, as yards continued to face pressure from weak domestic steel demand, high financing costs and currency depreciation. Buying prices remain relatively uncompetitive compared with India, Bangladesh and Pakistan, limiting Türkiye’s ability to attract conventional recycling tonnage. Nevertheless, Türkiye maintains a competitive position in recycling EU-linked vessels, supported by its proximity to Europe and established environmental compliance standards. Overall, market sentiment remains selective, with limited expectations of a significant recovery in recycling activity in the near term”, the company’s report concluded. Meanwhile, in a separate note, shipbroker Intermodal said that “last week, ship recycling market was steady, though sentiment diverged across the four main destinations. Bangladesh is leading on consistent buying appetite and India remained resilient, while Pakistan and Turkey stayed subdued. Alang remains firm. Local steel market continues to be slow, amid the Diwali festive period, with prices moving lower. Local currency appreciated, though, against the USD, after the US mid-term elections. Candidate tonnage on offer remained scarce. On the policy front, the European Parliament’s Environmental Committee voted against the proposal to include the 2 Indian yards on the EU approval list, citing concerns over beaching methods, although a final decision is still pending. Source: Intermodal shipbroker Chattogram continues to have a positive sentiment, with a steady buying interest in conventional tonnage. Local steel prices increased, though the steel market still lacks clear direction. Local currency weakened further against the USD, as state-backed entities progressed with sizeable payments for oil imports, adding to local demand for USD. On the waterfront, only limited number of vessels were circulated. The onset of the dry season, coupled with an expectation of recovery in construction, could provide support for steel consumption and yard activity. Gadani remained unchanged, with no urgent appetite for tonnage amid slow local markets. Domestic plate prices are holding steady, while grey-market imports of Iranian steel weigh on breakers. Local exchange rate was also broadly stable. Waterfront activity remained thin. In policy, Pakistan reached to 6 authorized ship recycling facilities by HKC and DASR requirements. Aliaga buyers remain selective amid weak transactional activity. The domestic market is still under pressure from cautious steel demand, currency depreciation and high inflation”. articles.body: Tankers In High Demand During October in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 O ctober’s secondhand market showed a clear shift towards tankers, despite little change in overall activity. A total of 168 vessels changed hands, unchanged year on year and 2% above September. Tanker sales rose 61% to 82 vessels, while dry bulk sales fell 30.5% to 57. Tankers accounted for 49% of all transactions, compared with 34% for dry bulk, with their gains offsetting fewer sales elsewhere. Disclosed investment across all sectors reached approximately US$4.7bn, below September’s US$6.6bn. Tankers attracted US$2.9bn, compared with US$1.1bn for dry bulk and US$0.7bn for other vessels. Their share was approximately 62% of total capital, rising to 73% within dry bulk and tankers alone. The stronger tanker weighting therefore accompanied a monthly decline in aggregate spending. Through October, total sales reached 1,481 vessels, up 17% year on year. Dry bulk retained the larger count, with 644 sales against 572 tankers, but tanker purchases grew 68%, compared with 7% for dry bulk. Tankers also attracted US$20.8bn of the US$32.1bn disclosed across these two sectors, versus US$11.3bn for dry bulk. Greek and Chinese buyers followed different patterns. Within dry bulk and tankers, Greek buyers purchased 16 ships in October, evenly split between the sectors; Chinese buyers purchased 12, comprising nine bulkers and three tankers. Over January–October, Greek capital favoured tankers, at US$4.5bn against US$2.1bn in dry bulk. Chinese investment was concentrated in dry bulk, at US$2.5bn versus US$0.6bn in tankers. Chinese capital was also more weighted towards older vessels, while Greek buyers showed a younger dry bulk mix. The overall picture is one of continued investment with the strongest expansion in tanker buying. Dry bulk remains active, but October’s weaker turnover points to a less uniform market. Whether this tanker concentration persists will depend on freight expectations and operating conditions; aggregate spending alone cannot establish rising values for comparable ships. The capesize index, which typically transports 150,000-ton cargoes, including iron ore and coal, climbed by 5.5% to a peak since October 5 at 4,700 points. Concurrently, the panamax index, which usually carries 60,000 to 70,000 tons of coal or grain, rose by 1.4% to its highest since October 23 at 2,103 points. articles.body: Shipping puts AI readiness to the test with new maturity benchmark in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 L loyd’s Register (LR) has expanded its Digital Maturity Index (DMI) benchmarking tool with a new AI maturity assessment, helping shipowners and operators evaluate their readiness for artificial intelligence as adoption accelerates across the maritime industry. Unveiled at Smart Maritime Network Singapore 2026, the enhanced DMI process introduces AI readiness benchmarking and sector-specific digital use cases while marking a milestone of more than 100 participating organisations. Developed to help maritime organisations benchmark their digital capabilities against industry peers, the DMI enables organisations to assess current capabilities, prioritise investment and accelerate progress towards their digital ambitions. Constantinos Chaelis, Gas Segment Director, LR The new AI maturity assessment examines the foundations required for successful AI adoption, including governance, workforce training, organisational culture, data readiness and performance measurement. It also assesses how AI is being applied across operational areas such as crew management, trade execution, vessel technical management and commercial functions. By looking beyond technology adoption alone, the assessment helps organisations identify whether they have the people, processes and data infrastructure needed to support AI-driven decision making and operational improvement. It also explores industry expectations, perceived opportunities and barriers to implementation. Eleanna Apostolidi, Head of DMI Product Innovation, LR, said: “Across the industry, we’re seeing organisations move beyond AI curiosity and into practical implementation. The challenge is that many companies are investing in AI before fully understanding whether their governance, data and internal capabilities are ready to support it. Eleanna Apostolidi, Head of DMI Product Innovation, LR “The DMI helps organisations establish that baseline. By introducing AI maturity benchmarking, we’re giving shipowners and operators a clearer view of where they are today and what they need to address before they can scale AI with confidence.” Alongside the AI assessment, LR has introduced a range of gas-sector-specific use cases, allowing LNG operators to benchmark the application of digital technologies against operational challenges including boil-off gas management, sloshing risk management, LNG cargo ageing prediction, rollover prevention, pump tripping mitigation, tank maintenance optimisation and brittle fracture monitoring. The additions reflect growing interest in how technologies such as analytics, automation, IoT and digital twins can support safer, more efficient and data-driven LNG operations. Constantinos Chaelis, Gas Segment Director, LR, said: “For LNG operators, digital transformation needs to be grounded in the operational realities of gas shipping. By embedding targeted LNG use cases into the Digital Maturity Index, LR is helping operators benchmark their digital readiness against the specific challenges they face, from cargo management and asset integrity to maintenance planning and operational performance. “The value of the DMI is that it gives the gas sector a structured way to understand where digital capability is already mature, where gaps remain and where investment can be focused to improve safety, efficiency and decision-making across LNG operations.” The DMI helps maritime organisations understand where they are on their digital transformation journey and identify where a clearer roadmap may be needed to turn insight into practical progress. The latest enhancements build on LR’s Digital Transformation Research Programme and support the industry’s transition towards increasingly connected and intelligent operations. articles.body: Global Shipping Report: October U.S. Container Imports Hit Record Volume in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 U.S. containerized imports totaled 2,674,808 twenty-foot equivalent units (TEUs) in October 2026, up 5.0% from September and 16.0% from October 2025. October marked the highest monthly volume on record, exceeding the previous high set in May 2022 by 2.0%. Through the first 10 months of 2026, imports increased 2.3% from the same period last year. China-origin imports rose for a fourth consecutive month to 987,805 TEUs, the highest monthly volume since January 2025. Imports from the top 10 countries of origin (CoO) increased 5.8% from September, with seven origins posting gains. East and Gulf Coast gateways gained share as Houston, Savannah, Norfolk, and Charleston increased volumes. Gulf Coast imports rebounded 24.0%, while port transit delays increased modestly at seven of the top 10 ports. Trade and routing conditions continue to change. U.S. officials extend the suspension of specified China-related maritime fees, the Panama Canal expanded transit availability, while carriers added Suez-transit services subject to security conditions. Continued Middle East shipping incidents remain a concern for affected trade lanes. For importers, shifting trade conditions reinforce the need to monitor trade policy and port performance, evaluate sourcing and routing alternatives, and maintain flexibility in shipment and inventory planning. U.S. container imports reach a new monthly high in October. U.S. containerized imports increased by 128,547 TEUs (5.0%) from September to 2,674,808 TEUs in October 2026 (see Figure 1). Volume was 16.0% higher than in October 2025 and 29.2% above October 2019. October exceeded the previous high of 2,622,465 TEUs set in May 2022 by 52,343 TEUs (2.0%), making it the largest monthly volume on record. Through October, U.S. container imports were 2.3% higher than in the first 10 months of 2025. October marked the second consecutive month where the year-to-date total exceeded the comparative period in 2025, following eight months where 2026 year-to-date volumes were below last year’s pace. Figure 1: U.S. Container Import Volume Year-over-Year Comparison Source: Descartes Datamyne™ September-to-October volumes increased in nine of the 11 years since 2016 (see Figure 2). October’s 5.0% growth was moderate within that historical pattern and followed declines of 1.0% in 2024 and 0.1% in 2025. The recurring October increase suggests a seasonal pickup, potentially supported this year by extended peak-season demand and uneven cargo arrival timing. October’s record total also built on already elevated September volumes, meaning a moderate monthly increase was sufficient to establish a new high. Figure 2: September to October U.S. Container Import Volume Comparison Source: Descartes Datamyne™ Top 10 U.S. port volumes rise as East and Gulf Coast entries gain. Combined imports across the top 10 U.S. ports increased 4.5% (98,272 TEUs) from September to October 2026 (see Figure 3). Houston posted the largest gain, up 26.7% (42,665 TEUs), followed by Savannah, up 12.6% (30,863 TEUs), Norfolk, up 17.7% (20,557 TEUs), and Charleston, up 18.6% (17,131 TEUs). New York, NY, increased 16.6% (9,081 TEUs), Tacoma 4.8% (3,292 TEUs), and New York/Newark (Newark, NJ) 0.3% (863 TEUs). October’s increases at Savannah, Houston, Norfolk, and Charleston followed declines at all four ports in September. Their combined volume rebounded 18.1% month-over-month but was just 3.6% above August, suggesting the large monthly gains partly reflect recovery from September’s lower volumes. Port data also shows China-origin cargo contributing materially, particularly at Houston and Savannah. Sustained peak-season demand and uneven vessel arrival timing may also have contributed to the rebound. Three West Coast ports declined: Los Angeles fell 1.4% (7,310 TEUs), Long Beach 2.0% (10,156 TEUs), and Oakland 10.9% (8,714 TEUs). The increases at East and Gulf Coast ports more than offset these decreases, indicating that October’s overall growth was uneven across gateways. Figure 3: September to October 2026 Comparison of Import Volumes at Top 10 U.S. Ports Source: Descartes Datamyne™ China-origin imports rise for a fourth consecutive month. U.S. containerized imports from China reached 987,805 TEUs in October 2026, increasing 63,351 TEUs (6.9%) from September and 183,904 TEUs (22.9%) from October 2025 (see Figure 4). October was China’s highest monthly volume since January 2025 and accounted for approximately half of the total U.S. month-over-month increase. China represented 36.9% of total U.S. container imports, up from 36.3% in September. Its October volume remained 3.4% below the July 2024 benchmark of 1,022,913 TEUs. China’s October import mix was led by plastics (HS-39), at 144,530 TEUs (14.6% of China-origin volume), furniture and bedding (HS-94), at 137,551 TEUs (13.9%), and toys, games, and sporting goods (HS-95), at 102,672 TEUs (10.4%). Machinery and electrical machinery (HS-84 and HS-85) accounted for a combined 18.0%, while apparel, made-up textiles, and footwear (HS-61 through HS-64) represented 9.4%. Notable year-over-year gains included plastics, up 30,040 TEUs (26.2%); toys, games, and sporting goods, up 25,185 TEUs (32.5%); articles of iron or steel (HS-73), up 19,240 TEUs (52.1%); and furniture and bedding, up 17,177 TEUs (14.3%). Figure 4: October 2025–October 2026 Comparison of U.S. Total and China-Origin Container Volumes Relative to the July 2024 China-Origin High Source: Descartes Datamyne™ Top 10 countries of origin increase from September. Imports from the top 10 CoO increased by 106,904 TEUs (5.8%) from September to October 2026 (see Figure 5). China led with an increase of 63,351 TEUs (6.9%), followed by South Korea, up 20,871 TEUs (22.8%), and Germany, up 11,808 TEUs (22.8%). Hong Kong added 6,644 TEUs (7.8%), Thailand 4,813 TEUs (4.3%), Indonesia 4,022 TEUs (6.5%), and Japan 1,044 TEUs (1.9%). Germany’s increase partially recovered September’s decrease of 15,212 TEUs. Vietnam fell 3,371 TEUs (1.2%), Taiwan 2,088 TEUs (3.6%), and India 191 TEUs (0.2%). October’s gains were spread across more countries than September’s, when China’s increase largely offset declines elsewhere. Figure 5: September to October 2026 Comparison of U.S. Import Volumes from Top 10 Countries of Origin Source: Descartes Datamyne™ All top 10 countries of origin grow year-over-year. Compared with October 2025, October 2026 imports from the top 10 CoO increased by 304,577 TEUs (18.5%) (see Figure 6). All CoOs posted year-over-year gains: China imports increased 183,904 TEUs (22.9%), approximately 60% of the group’s net gain. South Korea added 22,324 TEUs (24.8%), Vietnam 21,898 TEUs (8.3%), Hong Kong 20,873 TEUs (29.5%), and India 19,540 TEUs (20.4%). Thailand increased 15,801 TEUs (15.6%), Germany 10,594 TEUs (20.0%), Indonesia 4,889 TEUs (8.0%), Taiwan 4,108 TEUs (7.9%), and Japan 647 TEUs (1.2%). Figure 6: October 2025 to October 2026 Comparison of U.S. Import Volumes from Top 10 CoO Source: Descartes Datamyne™ East and Gulf Coast gateways gain share in October. The top five East and Gulf Coast gateways accounted for 39.9% of total U.S. container imports in October 2026, up 3.2 percentage points from the September share of 36.7% (see Figure 7). The top five West Coast gateways accounted for 44.9%, down 2.1 percentage points from 47.0%. Together, the top 10 ports handled 84.8% of U.S. imports, up 1.1 percentage points from September’s 83.7%. Figure 7: September to October 2026 Comparison of U.S. Import Volumes from Top 10 Countries of Origin Source: Descartes Datamyne™ Port transit delays increase modestly at seven of top 10 ports. U.S. container imports have exceeded 2.5 million TEUs in each month since July 2026, while transit delays have increased progressively. The unweighted average across the 10 tracked gateways rose from 4.2 days in June to 4.6 in July, 5.5 in August, 6.0 in September, and 6.3 in October—approximately 50% above June. Nine of the 10 gateways recorded higher delays over that period. October’s modest monthly increase therefore followed several months of accumulating delays, suggesting that sustained high volumes may already be contributing to pressure on the inland logistics network. November’s data will help indicate whether that pressure continues to intensify.Figure 8: Monthly Average Transit Delays (in days) for the Top 10 Ports (August–October 2026) Source: Descartes Datamyne™ Note: Descartes’ definition of port transit delay is the difference, measured in days, between the Estimated Arrival Date initially declared on the bill of lading and the date when Descartes receives the U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP)-processed bill of lading data. Changes are calculated before rounding. Gulf Coast imports rebound above their 12-month average. Gulf Coast container imports rose to 266,905 TEUs in October 2026, up 51,582 TEUs (24.0%) from September and 19.7% from October 2025 (see Figure 9). October was 16.2% above the rolling 12-month average of 229,711 TEUs and the highest month since the report began tracking this statistic in August 2023. Houston’s increase of 42,665 TEUs represented approximately 83% of the region’s net monthly gain. However, Houston’s volume had declined 16.5% in September, leaving October imports 5.8% above August and suggesting that the substantial monthly increase partly reflects recovery from September’s lower base. Higher China-origin volumes also contributed to Houston’s rebound. articles.title: Midterms strip out the war premium, but the next two months make shorts a risky bet
articles.summary: Crude futures have just posted their sharpest sell-off since 2020. Brent fell 16.6% between the 30 October peak and 4 November. On that day the January contract settled at $94.62/bbl after an $8.98/bbl drop. The trigger was the Democrats’ sweep of both chambers of Congress, which the market read as raising pressure...
articles.body: Midterms strip out the war premium, but the next two months make shorts a risky bet in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 Crude futures have just posted their sharpest sell-off since 2020. Brent fell 16.6% between the 30 October peak and 4 November. On that day the January contract settled at $94.62/bbl after an $8.98/bbl drop. The trigger was the Democrats’ sweep of both chambers of Congress, which the market read as raising pressure on Washington to wind down the war with Iran. Trend-following CTAs amplified the move, selling around 126 mbbl across crude and products since 30 October, including 52 mbbls on 4 November alone. Brent has since rebounded to around $97/bbl amid fresh tanker incidents in the Hormuz Strait, and prompt spreads have firmed, but it remains on course for a weekly loss of roughly 12%. The sell-off confirms what we flagged in The Crude View and this month’s House View: the war’s price had moved out of the barrel and onto paper, as futures had always been where geopolitical risk premium sits. October was the heaviest month of the war, with 35 vessel attacks. Even so, crude flows exiting the region remained high, averaging 16.6 mbd in October (excluding Iranian oil), down 500 kbd against 17.1 mbd September and also against pre-war flows. Physical weakness has also deepened, as our latest weekly crude report shows. The DFL spread collapsed from as much as +$18/bbl to +$1.70/bbl over the month (Argus) and the North Sea Dated M1-M2 spread fell to -$3.20/bbl on 4 November, its weakest since May 2020. Dubai M1-M2 flipped into contango for the first time since mid-July, and Murban’s premium to Dubai swaps shrank to $4.50/bbl from more than $30/bbl in mid-September (Argus). Aramco cut its December Arab Light OSP to Asia by $2/bbl to a six-year low, below the market at roughly Oman/Dubai -$7/bbl. Freight explains part of this. With PG-China averaging a record $36.60/bbl in October, the freight bill has replaced quality as the thing a differential measures. Sellers inside the Persian Gulf discount to pay it, and grades that cannot pass it on trade at multi-year lows. But freight is not the whole story: Atlantic rates are now falling fast, yet Tupi and Bonny Light arbitrage economics into Asia worsened by around $10/bbl week on week as Dubai’s structure weakened. The underlying driver is supply. Our balances show a 1.1 mbd crude surplus in Q4, the first quarterly surplus this year, as Middle Eastern barrels return. That said, being short futures here is risky. Dated is now trading around $96/bbl, about $9/bbl below our November base case of $105/bbl. The geopolitical risk premium is composed of two layers and prices currently are between the two. First, the risk premium associated with heightened attacks or threats of attacks. Second, the overall distance between the two parties to end the war. The first layer seems to have come out due to the talk of mediation, but the market knows a deal is still needed to resolve the situation. Credible de-escalation headlines could push them lower, but escalation risk is concentrated in the next two months, the window our Compass series laid out in Lame Duck or Angry Duck. Diplomacy is active on the de-escalation path. Trump discussed Qatar’s mediation with its Emir on 6th November, and Washington is reviewing an Iranian nuclear proposal. Doha is also reportedly circulating a two-step plan that would trade the end of the US blockade and some frozen funds for IAEA access and a Hormuz reopening. But Tehran insists Washington must first meet its seven conditions, including sanctions relief, a US withdrawal from the region and reparations. This indicates the two sides are still too far apart. Meanwhile, the more the US waits, the more economic pressure Tehran will feel. Iran has not loaded a crude cargo since 25 August, and we expect its oil revenues (from crude and condensate sales) to hit zero by mid-December. That cliff may raise the risk of further attacks as much as it pushes Tehran towards a deal. On the military side, there are reports that CENTCOM is finalising plans for major combat operations, though no order has been given. The USS Theodore Roosevelt, in Singapore this week, could reach the region from mid-November. Israeli defence officials, for their part, see no major US build-up yet. The outgoing Congress sits until 3 January. After that, Senate leader Chuck Schumer, who has pledged “we will end the war” with some Republican support, will control war powers votes and funding. President Trump will still benefit veto powers, but the window to act militarily will narrow down post-January. Trump’s personality also needs to be accounted for: he could be looking to authorise a strike to later claim victory, or may push further to save his foreign policy legacy. Positioning adds to the asymmetry. Trend CTAs have cut Brent exposure from maximum long to 36% long, meaning a portion of managed money length has gone. However, even in a de-escalation scenario, depleted inventories and US/Chinese restocking should keep a floor near $70/bbl. With physical markets already long but geopolitical risk concentrated before January, heavy short exposure remains highly risky until that window closes. articles.title: Eni, Fincantieri and RINA present the second edition of the Sustainable Maritime Transport Outlook
articles.summary: Eni, a global energy company, Fincantieri, a global leader in the construction of high-complexity ships, and RINA, the global inspection, certification and consulting engineering multinational group, today presented in Rome the second edition of the Sustainable Maritime Transport Outlook, developed with the technical...
articles.body: Eni, Fincantieri and RINA present the second edition of the Sustainable Maritime Transport Outlook in International Shipping News 12/11/2026 Eni, a global energy company, Fincantieri, a global leader in the construction of high-complexity ships, and RINA, the global inspection, certification and consulting engineering multinational group, today presented in Rome the second edition of the Sustainable Maritime Transport Outlook, developed with the technical support of Bain & Company Italy. The Outlook provides a global overview of solutions for decarbonising maritime transport, comparing different technology and fuel options in terms of their emissions reduction potential, maturity, infrastructure availability and the evolution of their Total Cost of Ownership through to 2050. The quantitative analysis is supported by a broad range of interviews with operators and stakeholders across the value chain, including shipowners and operators representing around 40% of the container market and 20% of the cruise market, engine and propulsion technology suppliers accounting for more than 80% of the ICE market, as well as ports and industry associations. Together, these interviews provide a clear picture of market realities. The key message emerging from this second edition is that the landscape is more uncertain than it was a year ago. However, competitive solutions are already available to reduce environmental impact today, offering a pragmatic response to the European regulations currently in force while the industry awaits global decisions from the IMO. Under the Outlook’s reference scenario, “Today as Future”, Europe is expected to achieve an 80% reduction in emissions intensity by 2050 compared with 2020 levels, while the reduction globally is projected at around 40%. The Outlook also considers a slower scenario, “Decarbonization by 2070”, under which the achievement of Europe’s decarbonisation targets is postponed until 2070, with countries in the rest of the world following several years later. Compared with last year, three of the four indicators shaping the transition, namely the regulatory framework, macroeconomic conditions, fuel and infrastructure availability, and technological maturity, have deteriorated, with regulatory uncertainty having the greatest impact. The global IMO agreement has been postponed and, when countries are weighted by tonnage, almost 90% support a more gradual pathway, while the United States has taken a position against maritime decarbonisation. Europe, by contrast, has reaffirmed the targets already established under FuelEU Maritime. The economic outlook has also become more uncertain due to slowing growth, tariffs and geopolitical tensions, while the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz is increasing risks to trade flows and the global economy. The low-emission hydrogen value chain has lost momentum, with numerous maritime projects put on hold. Technology nevertheless continues to play an enabling role, with the orderbook for alternative-fuel vessels growing slowly but steadily. However, against a backdrop of uncertainty, shipowners are increasingly favouring mature, readily available solutions. Synthetic fuels produced from green hydrogen will be essential to complete the pathway to net zero, but they remain expensive and depend on a supply chain that has yet to be fully developed. Through Enilive, Eni is among the leaders in the production of HVO biofuels from renewable feedstocks. These fuels are not only a solution for contributing to decarbonisation, but also an important component of industrial strategy and a means of strengthening the resilience of the production system. Alongside LNG and bio-LNG, biofuels can support maritime transport decarbonisation by leveraging already existing vessels and infrastructure. However, to fully unlock their potential and help the maritime sector progress towards climate neutrality, a regulatory framework is needed that recognises their role across all transport sectors, together with pragmatic and stable operational rules that can support investment development. Fincantieri supports shipowners on their decarbonisation journey through a pragmatic and flexible approach, integrating different technologies and developing innovative solutions. In the cruise sector, LNG is currently the leading alternative fuel, paving the way for progressive decarbonisation through bio-LNG and, in the longer term, e-LNG. Biofuels such as HVO and dual-fuel propulsion systems further broaden the range of available options. At the same time, the Group is working to improve the efficiency of the ship as an integrated system and is developing new energy and propulsion solutions, while also exploring longer-term opportunities through research into nuclear technologies. RINA contributes to the decarbonisation of maritime transport by providing operators across the value chain with its engineering and technological expertise, supporting them in identifying and adopting the most effective solutions. In particular, the Group assesses the technological maturity, practical feasibility and environmental performance of different alternatives, while helping to verify their compliance with regulatory requirements. The Outlook therefore sets out concrete commitments for every player across the value chain: common rules and standards for regulators and certification bodies; targeted investment and flexible infrastructure for ports; availability and diversification for fuel suppliers; vessels designed to accommodate multiple solutions and retrofit support for shipyards and shipowners; and continued investment in research and development by engine manufacturers. Pragmatism does not mean waiting: it means starting with mature technologies while building platforms that can evolve over time. Against the backdrop of an increasingly complex geopolitical environment, Eni, Fincantieri and RINA also formalised their commitment during the event to continue the Observatory’s work for the next three years. The signing of the agreement marks the first step in a collaborative journey that is expected to deepen and become increasingly strategic, with the potential to involve additional players across the value chain in the future. The cost landscape changes over time in Europe, where progressive decarbonisation targets are underpinned by a system of increasing penalties. In 2030, fossil fuels remain the most cost-effective options, while synthetic fuels can cost around three times as much. From 2040 onwards, European emissions penalties make biofuels increasingly competitive, and by 2050 fossil fuels could cost around twice as much as the more sustainable alternatives. Looking at Europe’s fuel mix in 2050, there is no single clear winner, but a well-defined backbone emerges: biofuels will account for around one third of the mix, alongside fossil and bio-LNG, while synthetic fuels will contribute around 20% to the decarbonisation pathway. Overall, this will result in an 80% reduction in GHG emissions compared with 2020 levels. Compared with the previous edition, the overall direction of the transition remains unchanged, but the projected contribution of synthetic fuels has been reduced by around half. As a result, the investment required to upgrade European port infrastructure is also lower: approximately $15 billion, compared with the roughly $25 billion estimated last year, with the entire difference attributable to the slower uptake of synthetic fuels. At global level, the transition is expected to progress more slowly. By 2050, the global fuel mix will still rely significantly on conventional fuels, which will account for around 70% of the total, while GHG emissions reductions will reach only around 40% compared with 2020 levels. In Europe, by contrast, biofuels and LNG will remain the main areas of convergence with the rest of the world, albeit within a faster emissions reduction pathway. In the cruise sector, which is of strategic importance to the Italian shipbuilding industry, synthetic fuels are expected to play a greater role than in maritime transport overall. This will primarily involve e-LNG, which could help decarbonise LNG-powered vessels already in the fleet while making the most of investments already made in existing platforms. Although nuclear propulsion is not expected to make a significant contribution to the 2050 decarbonisation pathway, the first nuclear-powered vessels could enter service between 2040 and 2045. Over the longer term, nuclear could also emerge as a key technology for certain high-power, long-range segments. This makes it important to begin research, assessment and development activities in this field today. Finally, the decarbonisation of maritime transport will require coordinated action across the entire value chain. Stakeholder interviews highlight a number of common barriers: regulatory uncertainty, which is holding back investment; the difficulty of passing the additional cost of lower-emission fuels on to customers; and bottlenecks that are more pronounced onshore than onboard vessels. Accelerating the transition will require a more stable global framework, consistent price signals, sufficiently predictable demand, reliable fuel volumes and greater feedstock diversification. articles.title: Freightos Weekly Update: LA/LB strike deadline extended; Dem win increasing trade uncertainty
articles.summary: Last week’s US midterm election results saw Republicans lose control of both houses of Congress, raising questions about possible implications for trade and logistics. On the one hand, the shift, reflecting voter concerns over inflation including from tariffs and energy prices, could mean the White House will seek to...
articles.body: Last week’s US midterm election results saw Republicans lose control of both houses of Congress, raising questions about possible implications for trade and logistics. On the one hand, the shift, reflecting voter concerns over inflation including from tariffs and energy prices, could mean the White House will seek to avoid introducing new tariffs and aim to deescalate the war in Iran in the hopes of bringing oil prices down. On the other hand, with President Trump likely to face difficulties passing new legislation, the election may embolden the president to focus and act on foreign and trade policy which is less easily influenced by Congress. In recent months the administration has trended toward deescalation in trade relations with China. And post the election late last week, both sides officially extended the pause on reciprocal port call fees until January 10th, aligning with the extension of the other elements of the interim US-China agreement announced back in September. Presidents Trump and Xi will meet in China next week. This year’s many trade war twists and turns may have helped drive the unusually early and then unusually long transpacific ocean peak season that has kept US container import volumes elevated since May. A lower effective tariff regime on many US trading partners including China following the Supreme Court’s IEEPA invalidation in February, and anticipation that duties would increase in July may have spurred some of the frontloading that started in May. But tariffs that stayed about level in July and beyond, IEEPA refunds that infused many importers with unexpected cash, and surprisingly resilient consumer spending may all have helped keep the rally going. The latest National Retail Federation US ocean import volume report shows container arrivals started climbing in May but continued their ascent through the summer peaking at just below record levels in September at 2.37 million TEU. Volumes are estimated to have eased 5% in October with November volumes projected to be down 14% from the September high. The report estimates that year totals will be 2.2% stronger than in 2025, following earlier expectations of flat volumes or even more modest growth. Slowing demand may be one factor in transpacific container rates easing slightly last week as significant carrier GRIs failed to materialize. But at $8,200/FEU to the West Coast and $9,700/FEU to the East Coast, prices are still at about peak levels. The ILWU Local 26 watchmen union has extended its strike deadline to November 20th to allow more time for negotiations with operators at the ports of LA and Long Beach with the aim of averting a potentially disruptive walk out. Though most holiday season merchandise has by now already arrived at the ports, a lot of goods still need to be moved inland, with a serious rail backlog slowing progress for many importers and making the prospect of a strike even more concerning. Carriers seem to have abandoned November 1st GRI hopes for Asia – Europe lanes as well, as prices dipped 5% last week to $3,400/FEU to North Europe and 1% to $4,300/FEU to the Mediterranean. Though rates aren’t climbing for now, prices are well above last year’s levels with N. Europe rates up 50% year on year and Mediterranean prices up 88%. Air rates out of the Far East continued to climb last week on peak season demand. China – US prices increased 3% to more than $8.00/kg, already reaching last year’s high that was hit only in mid-December 2025. China – Europe rates increased 11% to $4.87/kg, and are up 23% year on year. Part of the rate strength is due to a higher floor, propped up by still-elevated jet fuel prices. For some lanes, especially many Far East – N. America routes, strong demand from data center hardware volumes has kept pressure on rates and also helped set the high starting point for peak season spot prices. Some observers speculate however that Democrat control over Congress could mean tighter AI regulations that could slow data center hardware volume growth to the US. Transatlantic air cargo rates have climbed by 33% over the last month to $2.90/kg as capacity reductions from winter schedules – as well as possible freighter shifts to higher volume lanes – and peak season demand combine to put pressure on rates. Best, Judah Levine, Head of Research Freightos Group (Nasdaq: CRGO)

articles.title: Geneva Dry: Belships’ Ivar Hansson Myklebust on China’s changing commodities role
articles.summary: Ivar Hansson Myklebust, chair and CEO of Norway’s Belships, believes the shipping industry continues to underestimate the growth potential of developing economies. Ahead of his appearance at Geneva Dry 2027, he discusses China’s changing trading patterns, fleet supply and the opportunities emerging across minor...
articles.body: Dry Cargo Europe Maritime CEO Geneva Dry: Belships’ Ivar Hansson Myklebust on China’s changing commodities role Splash November 12, 2026 0 206 2 minutes read Ivar Hansson Myklebust, chair and CEO of Norway’s Belships, believes the shipping industry continues to underestimate the growth potential of developing economies. Ahead of his appearance at Geneva Dry 2027, he discusses China’s changing trading patterns, fleet supply and the opportunities emerging across minor bulks. A changing China, resilient emerging economies and a relatively predictable fleet supply picture will be among the biggest themes shaping dry bulk shipping when the industry gathers in Geneva next April, according to Ivar Hansson Myklebust. The Belships chief is cautiously optimistic about the outlook for minor bulks, arguing that developing economies continue to generate more trade than many shipping forecasts anticipate. “We tend to underestimate both the economic growth and physical trade volumes originating to and from developing countries,” Myklebust says. He believes this trend will continue to support the handysize and supramax markets. “The positive development in trade volumes for most minor bulks is due to this development, and on the balance I think this effect will be with us for some time.” Myklebust brings considerable industry experience to the discussion. Before joining Belships, he headed OMP Management and held senior leadership positions at Höegh Autoliners and Norden. He also chaired Gram Car Carriers until its acquisition by MSC. Looking ahead to Geneva Dry, he identifies the balance between future fleet supply and underlying demand as a central issue. “We have uncertainties galore regarding demand development now, while the fleet demographics are pretty well-known for the next three to four years,” he observes. Geopolitical disruption remains another major concern, particularly following the deadly attacks on merchant shipping in the Black Sea and Arabian Gulf “I sincerely hope that the hostilities that have caused tragic seafarer casualties both in the Black Sea and the Arabian Gulf have come to an end or at least calmed down significantly by then. Fingers crossed,” he says. China’s changing role in dry bulk shipping is another development he believes deserves closer attention. “From being an almost sole importer of dry cargoes it has emerged into a large exporter over the last few years, a very interesting development indeed,” he says. The shift is altering demand for geared bulk carriers in the Pacific, adding new dimensions to the traditional trade patterns that have underpinned the sector for decades. Whether China’s growing export role continues will be an important question for owners positioning their fleets. On technology, Myklebust sees opportunities less in revolutionary developments than in improving everyday shipping processes, from maintenance planning to freight collection. Myklebust will join the Minor Bulks panel at Geneva Dry on Wednesday, April 28, alongside Emilie Nourry of Eramet, Malgorzata Gill of Holcim Trading, S.K. Lim of G2 Ocean and Vincenzo Romeo of Nova Marine Carriers. Braemar’s global head of dry research, Derek Langston, will moderate. For Myklebust, the value of Geneva Dry lies in bringing together the different sides of the commodities shipping business. “Hearing the differing views and opinions from key players from the horses’ mouth is always interesting,” he says. “And meeting market participants from all sides of the business is never a waste of time.” Geneva Dry 2027, the world’s premier commodities shipping conference, takes place at the Hotel President Wilson on April 27 and 28 with organisers today unveiling limited special discount rates at the five-star hotel for signed-up delegates. A new study says the United States has enough spare ethanol production capacity to supply a meaningful share of the global marine fuel market, offering shipowners another fuel option as the number of methanol-capable vessels continues to grow. The report, Marine Ethanol: Unlocking the US Opportunity , published Wednesday by the Maritime Ethanol & Methanol Alliance (MEMA), argues that ethanol could be used in existing methanol dual-fuel engines and bunkering infrastructure with relatively minor modifications, potentially easing concerns over the availability of low-emission methanol. According to the study, more than 300 methanol-capable vessels are already operating or on order, creating a potential market for ethanol either as a standalone marine fuel or blended with methanol. The United States is particularly well-positioned to meet that demand. U.S. ethanol plants have an annual production capacity of approximately 18.5 billion gallons, compared with actual production of 16.4 billion gallons in 2025, leaving roughly 2 billion gallons of unused capacity. The country already accounts for slightly more than half of global fuel ethanol production and exports to approximately 80 countries, supported by an established distribution network that includes Gulf Coast terminals near major bunkering hubs. The study estimates that supplying just 1% of shipping’s annual fuel consumption by mass would require approximately 1 billion gallons of ethanol, an amount that could be covered by existing U.S. spare capacity. A 5% market share by the mid-2030s would require around 5 billion gallons annually, necessitating additional production or a shift in existing demand. The findings come as ethanol begins moving beyond demonstration projects and into commercial shipping operations. In September, A.P. Moller-Maersk completed the first publicly announced commercial ship-to-ship ethanol bunkering of a deep-sea containership in the United States. The operation involved the dual-fuel Tangier Maersk , which received U.S.-produced corn ethanol in Houston. As gCaptain reported at the time, the operation was intended to provide practical experience with ethanol sourcing, handling, bunkering and onboard use as Maersk explores additional fuel options for its growing fleet of alcohol-capable vessels. Engine developer WinGD subsequently confirmed that the vessel successfully sailed from Houston to New York using ethanol, marking the first in-service operation of its X-DF-M/E alcohol-fuel engine platform on the fuel. The new study rates ethanol’s technology readiness at level 8–9, indicating that the underlying technology is mature, although widespread commercial deployment remains at an early stage. It also highlights ethanol’s potential to reduce conventional air pollutants compared with heavy fuel oil. According to the report, ethanol virtually eliminates sulfur oxide emissions, reduces nitrogen oxides by 40% to 94%, depending on engine technology, and cuts particulate matter by 90% to 99%. Those reductions concern emissions from fuel combustion rather than ethanol’s overall lifecycle greenhouse gas footprint, which depends on feedstock, production methods and supply-chain emissions. The study also identifies potential cost advantages. It estimates ethanol’s net production cost, after accounting for revenue from co-products, at less than $1 per gallon, although that figure does not represent the delivered price of marine fuel. Despite those advantages, significant hurdles remain before ethanol can become a widely traded marine fuel. These include developing consistent fuel specifications, establishing reliable certification and traceability systems, and ensuring that ethanol can meet the environmental requirements of emerging shipping regulations. “Ethanol is moving beyond pilots, and this study shows the United States has the production base and export infrastructure to supply shipping at scale,” said Clarence Woo, managing director of the Global Centre for Green Fuels. “The next challenge is consistency. As international bunkering grows, shipping needs standardised and fungible marine fuel specifications, together with traceable feedstocks and a robust chain of custody, so that ethanol from different producers and regions can be used with confidence.” The study arrives as the International Maritime Organization prepares for another round of negotiations over its proposed Net-Zero Framework. The IMO’s Marine Environment Protection Committee is scheduled to meet from November 30 to December 3, with a resumed extraordinary session provisionally planned for December 4, subject to confirmation. The discussions could influence how alternative fuels are assessed and rewarded under future international shipping emissions rules. For U.S. ethanol producers, the marine fuel market represents a potential new source of demand, while shipowners could gain access to an established fuel supply chain without waiting for production of renewable methanol to expand. However, the study’s projections remain illustrative, and the extent to which ethanol can compete with other marine fuels will depend on its delivered cost, lifecycle carbon intensity, regulatory treatment and commercial acceptance. The report was published by MEMA, a platform of the Singapore-based Global Centre for Green Fuels. Classification society ABS provided technical analysis as a knowledge partner, while U.S. ethanol producer Marquis Energy contributed industry input. The findings and recommendations are those of MEMA. articles.title: Maersk opens new logistics consolidation centre in Indonesia
articles.summary: Maersk has inaugurated a new consolidation centre in Semarang, Indonesia, expanding its warehousing and cargo handling capabilities in Central Java as the region continues to develop as a manufacturing and export hub. The new facility covers more than 16,000 square metres and offers 15,800 cubic metres of storage...
articles.body: Maersk has inaugurated a new consolidation centre in Semarang, Indonesia, expanding its warehousing and cargo handling capabilities in Central Java as the region continues to develop as a manufacturing and export hub. The new facility covers more than 16,000 square metres and offers 15,800 cubic metres of storage capacity, with 11,300 pallet positions arranged across a six-level racking system. Located approximately four kilometres from the Port of Tanjung Emas, the centre is designed to connect warehousing operations with container depot services, inland transportation and Maersk’s international shipping network. The Semarang Consolidation Centre operates under a Pusat Logistik Berikat (PLB), or Bonded Logistics Centre, licence, allowing customers to manage cargo within a customs-controlled environment. The arrangement supports inventory management and cargo consolidation, providing manufacturers with additional flexibility in coordinating shipments with production schedules and export requirements. Central Java has become an increasingly important manufacturing location for industries including footwear, garments and furniture. The development of export-oriented production in the region has increased demand for warehousing, customs services and inland connections capable of linking manufacturing sites with international markets. Strengthening logistics connections in Central Java The new centre is located approximately 300 metres from Maersk’s container depot and ten kilometres from the local airport. Its proximity to existing container handling facilities is intended to improve access to empty equipment and depot services, while inland transport connections provide options for moving cargo through other gateways when required. Maersk currently operates more than 128,000 square metres of warehousing space across 15 locations in Indonesia, alongside ocean freight, inland transportation, customs clearance and cargo consolidation services. “Bringing warehousing, depot, inland and ocean capabilities closer to their manufacturing base gives customers greater flexibility and a simpler, more connected way to manage their supply chains,” said Elaine Low, Managing Director of Maersk South East Asia. The investment forms part of Maersk’s efforts to expand its logistics infrastructure near manufacturing centres and strengthen connections between inland production areas and international shipping routes. By combining bonded warehousing with nearby depot facilities and transport services, the Semarang centre is expected to provide exporters with additional options for managing cargo before shipment through Indonesia’s maritime gateways.

articles.title: Russian Diesel Faces U.S. Buyer Resistance Despite Trump Sanctions Waiver
articles.summary: US companies are unlikely to import Russian diesel as a tanker full of the fuel idles off the US Eastern Seaboard, experts said, despite President Donald Trump's temporary waiver of some sanctions on Moscow's fuel exports.

Join the leading maritime news network Stock Photo: Shutterstock/bob63 By Arathy Somasekhar, Lisa Baertlein and Nicole Jao HOUSTON, Nov 11 (Reuters) – US companies are unlikely to import Russian diesel as a tanker full of the fuel idles off the US Eastern Seaboard, experts said, despite President Donald Trump’s temporary waiver of some sanctions on Moscow’s fuel exports. Banks are likely to be reluctant to finance US deals for Russian diesel, the experts said, noting there are legal questions about whether the president’s waiver is enough to allow for the imports. There are also operational challenges, because importers would need to blend the Russian diesel to meet US heating oil specifications. US lawmakers from both parties objected last month, when Trump temporarily waived parts of a law that slapped Moscow with sanctions after its invasion of Ukraine. Former President Joe Biden imposed the sanctions after the 2022 invasion, and Congress later backed them and codified them as law. Looking to lower diesel prices that spiked during the US-Israeli war on Iran, Trump’s plan would allow Russia to immediately export 300,000 tons, or 2.25 million barrels, of diesel to US and global markets. This would be followed by 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” The price of diesel in the US was $6.13 per gallon on Wednesday, according to the American Automobile Association. That is down 20 cents a gallon from $6.33 the day that Trump waived the sanctions in October but up 63% from $3.76 before the US-Israeli war on Iran began in late February, according to AAA data. A tanker carrying the first cargo of Russian diesel for the US halted its voyage off the East Coast this week, shipping data showed on Tuesday. Its operator said the destination had not yet been decided. On Tuesday, US Energy Secretary Chris Wright said he was confident the idled tanker would help supply global markets even if it did not land at a US port. “We just want that diesel going into the world markets,” Wright told reporters at an event in New Orleans. Last month, the US Treasury Department issued a general license temporarily permitting imports of Russian diesel. But any buyers could damage their reputation and also face legal risks if they engage in such “prohibited but authorized transactions,” said Jeremy Paner, a partner at law firm Hughes Hubbard & Reed and a former US sanctions official. Paner said any savings from buying cheaper Russian diesel could easily be wiped out by the need to pay hundreds of thousands of dollars in legal fees from likely upcoming congressional investigations. “It’s a relatively easy call for businesses to say, ‘We don’t want to touch it,’” Paner said. POLITICAL BLOWBACK Dozens of US senators, including six Republicans, have called on Trump to rescind ?the deal, saying it helps Russia fund attacks on Ukraine and has no benefit to Americans. New Jersey’s Democratic Governor Mikie Sherrill has warned local port officials and terminal operators against accepting Russian diesel, saying those shipments would break federal law. A handful of laws prohibit importing Russian oil products, analysts and lawyers said. Several jurisdictions, including the UK and the EU, also sanction Russian crude and fuel. US Representative Jamie Raskin of the House Judiciary Committee said in a letter that importers would remain liable “long after the current administration leaves office.” The letter to oil industry groups and the US Chamber of Commerce cited a 10-year statute of limitations. “Your members are now on notice that taking part in any effort to help President (Vladimir) Putin hawk Russian diesel in the US is a clear and dangerous violation of federal law,” he wrote. A Trump administration official said the temporary waiver was in compliance with all applicable laws. Still, finding a willing US importer might prove difficult. Banks are unlikely to finance deals related to a Russian diesel trade, which could violate sanctions in other countries, said David Tannenbaum, director of sanctions consultancy Blackstone Compliance Services and a former US Treasury sanctions specialist. “The money that’s on the table for a single deal in comparison to the compliance costs and potential headaches, I would be a hard pass,” he said, adding that every party downstream that touches the cargo and distributes it was a potential subject for an investigation in the US Congress. The Russian diesel would also need to be blended to meet New York Mercantile Exchange heating oil specifications, adding another deterrent for importers, Natalia Losada, an analyst at Energy Aspects, wrote in a note, adding that cargoes may still end up diverting to Brazil or other more traditional destinations for Russian diesel. “If the first vessel is unable to dock or discharge in any US ports, that does create that bit of a hurdle for every further vessel that is on its way,” said Janiv Shah, a vice president at consultancy Rystad Energy. articles.summary: OPEC+ crude oil production jumped in October, led by a sharp increase in output from Saudi Arabia despite continued disruption to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the Iran war.The OPEC+ group, which includes the Organization…
articles.body: OPEC+ Oil Production Rises in October, Nearing Pre-Iran War Rates Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 11, 2026 © CURIOS - stock.adobe.com OPEC+ crude oil production jumped in October, led by a sharp increase in output from Saudi Arabia despite continued disruption to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz caused by the Iran war. The OPEC+ group, which includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as Russia, pumped 41.23 million barrels per day in October, OPEC said in a monthly report on Wednesday, up about 2.04 million bpd from September. The figures, based on secondary sources, add to signs that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports by using workarounds such as ship-to-ship transfers to bypass disruption caused by the conflict. According to Reuters calculations based on OPEC data, October output was equivalent to 97% of the 42.72 million bpd produced by OPEC+ in February. Saudi Arabia told OPEC it pumped 10.563 million bpd in October, the report said, up from 8.372 million bpd in September. That was its highest output since February, when it reported production of 10.882 million bpd. Riyadh sharply increased its production in February ahead of US and Israeli strikes on Iran. Saudi Arabia has frequently intervened in oil markets, boosting supply during disruptions or curbing output when it sees a risk of oversupply. RUSSIAN OUTPUT ALSO RISES Russia's oil production rose by 41,000 bpd in October from September to 8.668 million bpd, according to the secondary sources cited in OPEC's report. US President Donald Trump last month announced an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Although the agreement failed to hold in any meaningful way, it provided a respite from Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries and may have supported oil output. OPEC left its forecasts for global oil demand growth unchanged after cutting them for six straight months, and made no changes to its 2027 outlook. The producer group expects world oil demand to rise by 2.55 million bpd next year to an average of 108.3 million bpd. It forecasts growth of 180,000 bpd in 2026. (Reuters)

November 11, 2026 © Adobe Stock/le Oil prices rose about 1% on Wednesday after dropping to two-month lows in the previous session, after Iran's security chief said Tehran would not allow any enriched nuclear material to leave the country. Washington has said nuclear matters must be part of any initial negotiations with Tehran aimed at ending the US-Israeli war on Iran. Brent futures were up $1.22, or 1.3%, at $92.71 a barrel by 1412 GMT. US West Texas Intermediate crude gained $1.09, or 1.3%, to $87.13. In the previous session, oil prices initially fell by more than $3 a barrel after US officials played down the need for further military strikes against Iran. Prices later pared some losses after an Iranian security official said no talks were taking place between the two sides. "Oil prices are being supported by fading hopes of an imminent de-escalation," UBS analyst Giovanni Staunovo said. There is little sign of attacks in the Strait of Hormuz easing after 37 ships were attacked in October, the highest monthly total since the start of the war, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. "There has been an increase of vessel attacks in the Gulf shipping lanes amidst uncertainty of the diplomacy talks," said June Goh, senior analyst at Sparta Commodities. She added that the key driver for the market was whether Iran would engage with US demands to reach a diplomatic agreement. Brent and WTI prices have fallen about 21% and 17%, respectively, since the start of the month on hopes of an end to the war. A tanker was struck northeast of Lima in Oman, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency said on Tuesday. Iran's Revolutionary Guards Navy said separately on Tuesday that two tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on an "unauthorized route" in the strait. "Even in the event a deal is struck, an increase in flows through the waterway would still depend on mine clearance, insurance costs and whether or not shipowners would even be willing to take the risk," LSEG Oil Research said in a November 10 note. On the supply side, US crude stocks rose by 9 million barrels in the latest week, market sources said, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute. Official data is due later on Wednesday. Data from Kpler shows that Middle East crude and condensate outages have dropped to about 3.8 million barrels per day, with Saudi and Iraqi crude output back to pre-war levels and outages in both countries down significantly. Separately, Vladimir Medinsky, Russia's chief negotiator on Ukraine, said on Wednesday that a peace settlement seemed to be closer after two days of talks in Abu Dhabi. A regional governor said a drone attack caused a fire in the port area of Ust-Luga on Russia's Baltic coast, injuring three workers. Russian oil refining capacity has been reduced by about 30% since late October following renewed Ukrainian drone attacks, industry sources said. articles.body: Hopes for Peace Continue Despite Ongoing Maritime Security Threats in the Middle East Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 11, 2026 © Adobe Stock/ImageBank4U In the Strait of Hormuz, tankers are still ablaze, oil spills are washing ashore and drones and missiles strike infrastructure across the region, despite expectations of a de-escalation reflected in falling oil prices. The United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported on Wednesday another incident involving a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz, while Iran said an oil tanker caught fire after hitting a naval mine. Reuters was unable to independently verify the reports. At least 10 ships were hit in the first 10 days of November, after 37 attacks in October, the highest monthly tally since the conflict began, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Videos posted on social media on Sunday and verified by Reuters showed a Navig8 tanker on fire near the coast of Oman. Iran claimed responsibility for hitting three tankers the same day for using "unauthorised routes" through the Strait of Hormuz. An image captured by the European Union's Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite on Sunday showed a large cloud of black smoke at the same location. Navig8, majority owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services, did not reply to emailed Reuters requests for comment. US forces have also continued to enforce a naval blockade of Iranian ports. A US military aircraft fired on and disabled a St Kitts-flagged cargo vessel that tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port on Saturday, US Central Command said. Attacks in the strait have caused environmental damage, with oil leaking from damaged tankers. A video shared on social media on Monday, and verified by Reuters, showed oil reaching the shores of Oman, while satellite imagery showed oil spills off the coast of Oman and UAE. The Omani government did not respond to Reuters request on Tuesday for comment on the video of oil reaching Omani shores. Elsewhere in the region, energy infrastructure and civilian facilities have also come under attack. The Iran-backed Houthis have struck targets including the offices of Saudi Aramco, the world's largest oil company. Video verified by Reuters showed damage to Aramco's office building in Riyadh, following Houthi-claimed missile strikes on November 8. The Saudi Energy Ministry said that a building belonging to Aramco in Riyadh had been targeted in an attempted attack, with debris causing limited damage to the building with no injuries or fatalities. The International Maritime Organization has confirmed 133 incidents, most of them attacks, in the region since the conflict began in late February, with at least 25 seafarers killed. (Reuters)

articles.body: Regional Container Lines (RCL) is preparing to introduce two new 7,000-TEU container vessels into its regional shipping network, with both ships scheduled for delivery in January 2027. The Thai container shipping company held naming ceremonies for KITIYA BHUM and LAKANA BHUM on 10 November in Shanghai, China, as part of its ongoing fleet renewal and expansion programme. The vessels are planned for deployment on RCL’s Korea Straits-India Service 2 (RKI2), which connects ports in South Korea, China, Malaysia, India and Pakistan, supporting container trade between Northeast Asia and the Indian Subcontinent. New vessels equipped with efficiency and emissions technologies According to RCL, both vessels have been built by Shanghai Waigaoqiao Shipbuilding (SWS), with naming ceremonies held at HantongWING Shipyard and Rongsheng Shipyard, respectively. Each vessel has a nominal capacity of 7,000 TEU and incorporates several technologies intended to improve operational efficiency and environmental performance.
