REUTERS/Ints Kalnins (Reuters) – Despite market bets on a de-escalation in the Iran war, new evidence has emerged in recent days of strikes on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and on energy infrastructure in the Middle East. On Tuesday, crude prices hit two-month lows after US officials downplayed the need for additional military action against Iran, with analysts noting President Donald Trump’s more conciliatory tone since the Republicans’ defeat in the November 3 midterm elections. However, there is little sign of attacks abating in November, after 37 ships were attacked in October, the highest monthly total since the start of the war, according to data from the Washington Institute for Near East Policy. Videos posted on social media on Sunday and verified by Reuters showed a Navig8 tanker on fire near the coast of Oman. An image captured by the European Union’s Copernicus Sentinel-2 satellite on Sunday showed a large cloud of black smoke at the same location. It was one of three tankers hit on Sunday for using “unauthorized routes” through the strait, Iranian state broadcaster IRIB reported, citing the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy. The vessel is managed by Navig8, majority owned by ADNOC Logistics & Services. Neither replied to emailed Reuters requests for comment. At the same time, US forces continued to enforce a naval blockade of Iranian ports. In the latest incident, a US military aircraft fired on and disabled a St Kitts-flagged cargo vessel that tried to depart regional waters after visiting an Iranian port on Saturday, US Central Command said. Attacks in the strait have caused environmental damage, with oil leaking from damaged tankers. A video shared on social media on Monday, and verified by Reuters, showed oil reaching the shores of Oman, while satellite imagery showed oil spills off the coast of Oman and UAE. The Omani government did not respond to Reuters request on Tuesday for comment on the video of oil reaching Omani shores. Elsewhere in the region, energy infrastructure and civilian facilities have also come under attack. Iran and its regional allies have struck targets including the offices of Saudi Aramco 2223.SE, the world’s largest oil company. Video verified by Reuters showed damage to Aramco’s office building in Riyadh, following Houthi-claimed missile strikes on November 8. The Saudi Energy Ministry said that a building belonging to Aramco in Riyadh had been targeted in an attempted attack, with debris causing limited damage to the building with no injuries or fatalities. The International Maritime Organization has confirmed 130 incidents, most of them attacks, in the region since the conflict began in late February, with at least 25 seafarers killed. Another tanker was struck northeast of Oman’s Lima, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said on Tuesday. UKMTO did not say who struck it. Iran’s Revolutionary Guards Navy said in a separate statement that two tankers caught fire after hitting naval mines on the “unauthorized route” in the strait. articles.title: Georgia emerges as a centre of excellence for automotive manufacturing and logistics
articles.summary: Georgia Ports Authority hosted its annual State of the Port of Brunswick, where CEO Griff Lynch and President Kevin Price reviewed market conditions and future plans. They pointed to the state’s success in attracting global automakers and building supply chains around them, following Audi’s recent announcement of a...
articles.body: Georgia Ports Authority hosted its annual State of the Port of Brunswick, where CEO Griff Lynch and President Kevin Price reviewed market conditions and future plans. They pointed to the state’s success in attracting global automakers and building supply chains around them, following Audi’s recent announcement of a factory in Georgia. Hyundai Motor Group’s Metaplant at Ellabell, 30 miles west of the Port of Savannah, occupies a 3,000-acre site and will create 8,500 jobs by 2031, with 22 suppliers already located nearby. Kia has run its flagship US plant at West Point on 2,200 acres since 2009. Rivian has broken ground on a USD 5 billion plant at Stanton Springs North, expected to create 7,500 long-term jobs by 2030, and has set up its East Coast headquarters in Atlanta. Audi plans to invest US$ 4 billion in its first US plant, near Macon, one of the brand’s largest production footprints globally, with about 4,500 jobs. Construction is due to start in 2027 and production in the early 2030s. BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Volvo, among others, use the Port of Brunswick for finished vehicle shipments and processing. The ports’ appeal to manufacturers and logistics providers rests on the combination of seaport access, dedicated rail, direct interstate links and proximity to Southeastern markets. Brunswick provides vehicle imports and exports, finished vehicle distribution, parts warehousing, manufacturing and vehicle processing. Savannah is a major gateway for containerised auto parts, with 40 vessel calls a week, 15,000 daily truck gate transactions and 42 double-stack trains a week from its on-dock Mason Mega Rail facility to inland markets via Norfolk Southern and CSX. Atlanta adds a major consumer market and distribution hub. Price also noted strong growth in heavy machinery such as construction and farm equipment. Lynch said Georgia Ports are creating opportunities for businesses to grow, strengthening supply chain competitiveness at state, regional, national and global levels and generating jobs. Chairman Alec Poitevint noted that Georgia has been named best state to do business for 13 consecutive years and that GPA is investing US$ 5 billion in infrastructure over the next ten years to meet future demand. Lynch and Price thanked GPA employees, the board, the ILA, customers and the local community.

articles.summary: Danish shipping giant AP Moller-Maersk has confirmed another cybersecurity breach after hackers gained access to an older IT system and extracted data, nearly a decade after the devastating NotPetya attack that cost the company up to $300m. articles.body: Containers Europe Maersk hit by fresh cyber breach Adis Ajdin November 12, 2026 0 548 1 minute read Cydome Cydome Danish shipping giant AP Moller-Maersk has confirmed another cybersecurity breach after hackers gained access to an older IT system and extracted data, nearly a decade after the devastating NotPetya attack that cost the company up to $300m. The Copenhagen-headquartered group said on Wednesday that the incident involved a local legacy system inherited through a previous acquisition. Maersk’s cybersecurity team launched an investigation after discovering the intrusion and has taken steps to secure the affected system.”Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed,” the company said. The carrier said the breach appeared to be confined to the legacy system, with no indication that other Maersk systems or those belonging to customers and partners connected through APIs and electronic data interchange (EDI) had been compromised. The company added that it does not expect disruption to customer operations, with its digital booking and shipment management platforms continuing to operate normally. Maersk has not identified the acquired business involved, disclosed what data was extracted or named those responsible for the intrusion. The announcement follows separate claims by a hacker group calling itself WhiteArmor that it had obtained around 100 GB of logistics data from a platform associated with LF Logistics, the Hong Kong-based logistics business Maersk acquired for $3.6bn in 2022. The group has reportedly demanded $5m in bitcoin. The claims remain unverified, and Maersk has not confirmed any connection between the alleged theft and the incident it is investigating. The latest breach brings back memories of June 2017, when the NotPetya malware attack crippled Maersk’s IT infrastructure and disrupted container shipping and terminal operations worldwide. The Danish group subsequently put the financial damage at between $250m and $300m, making it one of the costliest cyber incidents in shipping history. REUTERS/Amr Alfiky/File Photo International Maritime Organization (IMO) Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez has called on governments to step up enforcement of international maritime regulations in the Strait of Hormuz, warning that unsafe shipping practices are adding to the risks facing seafarers amid the ongoing conflict. In a statement issued Wednesday, Dominguez raised concerns about vessels transiting the strategic waterway without complying with basic international safety requirements, including provisions of the International Convention for the Safety of Life at Sea (SOLAS). The warning comes as commercial shipping continues to face attacks in and around the Strait of Hormuz, where the IMO has now verified more than 130 incidents involving merchant vessels since the conflict began on February 28. At least 25 seafarers have been killed, while others remain missing or have been injured. “IMO’s technical and operational regulations are there to protect seafarers, ships and the marine environment. They must be respected and enforced effectively,” Dominguez said. The IMO chief specifically cited reports of substandard vessels, ships concealing their IMO identification numbers, vessels operating under fraudulent registrations or false flags, and other unsafe practices. The concerns add another dimension to the shipping crisis in the Persian Gulf, where vessels already face significant security risks from ongoing hostilities. Dominguez’s comments highlight the need for governments to enforce existing maritime regulations even as the conflict complicates commercial navigation. He called on flag states, port states and coastal states to take action against violations within their respective jurisdictions and in accordance with international law. “I strongly urge shipowners and operators to refrain from commercial activities in the Strait that expose seafarers to unacceptable risks,” Dominguez said. The latest appeal follows last week’s meeting of the IMO Council in London, where member states called for stronger protections for seafarers and reiterated that vital shipping lanes must remain open, safe and secure. During the November 2–6 meeting, the Council condemned attacks on merchant shipping and called on governments to refrain from unlawful measures that endanger seafarers and international navigation. According to the IMO’s latest incident records, 133 incidents had been confirmed as of November 10, with 25 seafarer fatalities. Dominguez also renewed his call for a political solution to the crisis, urging governments to restore a safe, internationally recognized framework for navigation through the Strait of Hormuz that preserves established rights and freedoms of navigation. He warned that the conflict’s consequences extend well beyond the maritime industry, contributing to higher living costs for millions of people worldwide. “It is imperative for Governments to tackle the root causes of this conflict,” he said. articles.summary: The Panama Canal is increasing its daily transit capacity to 34 vessels and restoring the maximum allowable draft at its Neopanamax locks to 50 feet, easing restrictions as improved water...

Join the leading maritime news network Photo courtesy Panama Canal Authority The Panama Canal is increasing its daily transit capacity to 34 vessels and restoring the maximum allowable draft at its Neopanamax locks to 50 feet, easing restrictions as improved water conditions provide some relief from concerns over another prolonged El Niño. The Panama Canal Authority (ACP) announced the changes in a November 9 advisory to shipping, citing improving lake levels, favorable hydrological forecasts and the effectiveness of water-saving measures implemented at the locks. The adjustment adds one daily booking slot for Super vessels at the Panamax locks, increasing availability in that category from 18 to 19. Total daily reservation capacity rises from 33 to 34 slots, including 24 at the Panamax locks and 10 at the larger Neopanamax locks. The ACP also raised the maximum authorized draft for Neopanamax vessels to 15.24 meters (50 feet), effective immediately and until further notice. The increase follows an October adjustment that raised the allowable draft to 49 feet. The latest changes mark another shift in the canal’s operating outlook after months of concern over deteriorating water conditions and the potential for a prolonged El Niño event. As gCaptain reported in September, canal officials had postponed a planned reduction in the Neopanamax draft limit to 47.5 feet after reassessing Gatun Lake levels and rainfall projections. At the time, the canal was maintaining a 48-foot draft limit while warning that below-normal precipitation could persist for months. The concerns followed the historic 2023–2024 drought , which forced the canal to sharply restrict vessel transits and drafts, disrupting global shipping schedules and sending some cargoes on longer routes. At the worst point of that drought, daily transit capacity fell to just 22 vessels. The waterway has faced additional pressure this year as disruptions in the Middle East have redirected shipping traffic toward Panama, increasing competition for available transit reservations, particularly among energy carriers. The additional Panamax booking slot will be introduced in stages. For transit dates November 12–17, it will be available through the canal’s auction system. For November 18–23, it will be offered through the Special Competition booking period. Beginning with November 24 transit dates, the slot will become available through the regular Second Competition Period. Despite the improved outlook, the ACP continues to emphasize the importance of advance reservations. Its Transit Reservation System remains the only way to guarantee a transit date, and vessels arriving without bookings could face substantial delays. The authority said it will continue monitoring rainfall, watershed conditions and lake levels, with further operational adjustments possible as conditions change. The latest increase offers shipping companies greater flexibility heading into the final weeks of 2026, although the canal’s ability to sustain the higher capacity will continue to depend on freshwater availability. Join the leading maritime news network Illustration courtesy Ocean Infinity The UK is moving ahead with a £90 million investment in autonomous underwater systems, advanced sensors and artificial intelligence to strengthen the Royal Navy’s ability to track Russian submarines and protect critical infrastructure in the North Atlantic. The initiative, known as Atlantic Net, is the first operational phase of the Royal Navy’s broader Atlantic Bastion programme, which aims to combine crewed warships and submarines with autonomous systems to improve underwater surveillance and counter potential threats to subsea communications cables, energy networks and shipping routes. The UK Ministry of Defence announced the investment Tuesday during the International Sea Power Conference in Oslo, Norway, alongside a framework agreement with UK-based marine robotics company Ocean Infinity Solutions. GOV.UK Under the arrangement, Ocean Infinity will serve as the Royal Navy’s commercial mission partner, helping develop and operate a network of autonomous and remotely operated systems capable of maintaining persistent surveillance across the North Atlantic. The system will combine underwater sensors, uncrewed platforms, communications technology and AI-powered data analysis to detect and track potentially hostile submarine activity. The information will provide Royal Navy warships and Astute-class attack submarines with earlier warnings and a clearer picture of threats beneath the surface. The programme is expected to become operational in 2027, according to UK Defence Minister Luke Pollard, who outlined the plans in a speech in Oslo. “The threats beneath the North Atlantic are changing, and we are changing with them,” Pollard said. “This investment gives the Royal Navy new technology to find threats earlier and protect our critical infrastructure, while also backing British business.” The investment comes amid growing concern among European governments and NATO allies over the vulnerability of underwater infrastructure, particularly communications cables and energy connections that are essential to both civilian economies and military operations. Atlantic Bastion is intended to expand the Navy’s ability to monitor these networks while strengthening anti-submarine warfare capabilities and supporting the protection of Britain’s nuclear deterrent. For Ocean Infinity, the agreement marks a significant expansion of its role in defense and maritime security. The company, which has developed autonomous and remotely operated marine systems for commercial operations, said Atlantic Net represents a shift toward sustained underwater surveillance using a combination of uncrewed, autonomous and smaller-crewed platforms. “The Royal Navy has been exploring how to move beyond traditional, heavily crewed fleets towards a broader mix of robotic and lean-crewed platforms,” said Joe Robinson, President of Solutions at Ocean Infinity. “Atlantic Net is that idea coming to life.” Ocean Infinity said its role will include integrating maritime platforms, underwater sensors, communications, remote operations and data services into a coordinated surveillance capability directed by the Royal Navy. Ocean Infinity The £90 million framework is also expected to support nearly 200 skilled jobs within Ocean Infinity and its immediate supply chain, according to the Ministry of Defence. The programme will operate alongside NATO and Joint Expeditionary Force allies, with the goal of expanding the scale and persistence of underwater surveillance across the North Atlantic. The announcement also forms part of a broader British push toward a hybrid naval fleet that uses autonomous technology to supplement traditional warships and submarines, allowing the Royal Navy to monitor larger areas without relying entirely on crewed vessels. articles.title: Eimskip posts 43.6% EBITDA growth in third quarter
articles.summary: Icelandic shipping and logistics company Eimskip reported a 43.6% year-on-year increase in EBITDA for the third quarter of 2026, supported by higher cargo volumes, stronger freight rates and operational efficiency measures, despite a sharp rise in fuel costs. The company’s quarterly revenue increased by 19.4%...
articles.body: Icelandic shipping and logistics company Eimskip reported a 43.6% year-on-year increase in EBITDA for the third quarter of 2026, supported by higher cargo volumes, stronger freight rates and operational efficiency measures, despite a sharp rise in fuel costs. The company’s quarterly revenue increased by 19.4% compared with the same period in 2025, while EBITDA rose by EUR 8.9 million. Eimskip attributed the improvement to stronger underlying operations and restructuring initiatives introduced during the second half of last year. The year-on-year EBITDA comparison was also influenced by a EUR 2.9 million loss associated with the sale of the vessel Lagarfoss in the third quarter of 2025. Liner volumes rise as network adjustments support operations Eimskip’s liner segment recorded a 13.8% increase in revenue, while transported volumes grew by 6.8%, supported by stronger exports of seafood and farmed fish from Iceland and the Faroe Islands. The company introduced a new connection between Tórshavn in the Faroe Islands and Rotterdam in August, including a call at Ålesund, Norway. The service was established to accommodate increasing farmed salmon production and demand for improved connections to European markets. Alongside the new route, Eimskip adjusted its Norwegian sailing schedule and reduced the number of vessels deployed on that service by one. Despite the improvement in liner operations, profitability remained limited, with the segment generating EBIT of approximately EUR 500,000 during the quarter. “Despite this improvement, profitability remains unsatisfactory,” said Vilhelm Már Thorsteinsson, CEO of Eimskip. Forwarding and logistics contribute to revenue growth Eimskip’s forwarding business recorded a 30% increase in revenue, driven by an 11.2% rise in transported volumes and higher international freight rates. Growth was particularly strong on routes connected to Asia. Revenue from logistics and agency services increased by 14.4%, primarily reflecting greater trucking activity in Iceland, increased warehousing operations and improved port-related results. The company’s new chilled and frozen storage facility in Denmark also contributed to the segment’s performance. Meanwhile, operating expenses increased by 16.7% year-on-year, reflecting higher activity levels, increased third-party transportation costs and rising oil prices. Vessel bunker expenses climbed by EUR 6.1 million, representing a 56% increase compared with the previous year. Eimskip noted that the increase remained below the 78% rise in market fuel prices, mainly due to the timing of bunker purchases. Efficiency measures deliver further savings Operational improvement initiatives introduced in the second half of 2025 generated EUR 3.3 million in benefits during the third quarter, including a positive EBITDA contribution of EUR 2.9 million. For the first nine months of 2026, these initiatives delivered EUR 9.4 million in benefits, including an EBITDA improvement of approximately EUR 8 million. The measures included the discontinuation of dedicated coastal sailings, reductions in vessel deployment and adjustments to the company’s wider operating structure. Eimskip also reported that results from associated companies increased to EUR 7.3 million, compared with EUR 3.5 million a year earlier, primarily reflecting a vessel sale by Elbfeeder in July. Looking ahead, the company expects a more balanced development in working capital during the fourth quarter, following increased requirements associated with higher activity levels in Q3. Eimskip said its priorities remain operational efficiency, cost control and maintaining reliable shipping and logistics services amid continued uncertainty in global markets.

articles.title: CMA CGM announces new surcharges for Mediterranean and Mauritius trades
articles.summary: CMA CGM has announced new Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) for container shipments from Asia to the Mediterranean, North Africa and Mauritius, with implementation dates scheduled for mid-to-late November 2026. The French shipping company will introduce charges of up to US$1,600 per 40-foot container on Asia–Mediterranean...
articles.body: CMA CGM has announced new Peak Season Surcharges (PSS) for container shipments from Asia to the Mediterranean, North Africa and Mauritius, with implementation dates scheduled for mid-to-late November 2026. The French shipping company will introduce charges of up to US$1,600 per 40-foot container on Asia–Mediterranean routes. Separate surcharges will apply to shipments from China and other Asian markets to Port Louis, Mauritius. Both measures will remain in effect until further notice. Asia–Mediterranean surcharge takes effect on 25 November From 25 November 2026, CMA CGM will apply a PSS of US$800 per 20-foot container and US$1,600 per 40-foot container on shipments from all major Asian ports to base ports in the Mediterranean and North Africa. The new charges will cover dry containers, refrigerated cargo, out-of-gauge (OOG) shipments and paying empty containers. The implementation date is based on the cargo loading date, with the surcharge remaining in place until further notice. The announcement follows CMA CGM’s earlier adjustments to Asia–Mediterranean freight rates and surcharges for November. The latest measure introduces a separate peak season charge for cargo moving on these routes. Mauritius shipments face revised peak season charges CMA CGM has also announced revised PSS levels for container shipments from the Far East to Port Louis, Mauritius, effective 15 November 2026. Cargo originating in China and its Special Administrative Regions will be subject to a surcharge of US$800 per TEU. Shipments from Northeast Asia and Southeast Asia will face a lower surcharge of US$500 per TEU. Both charges apply to all cargo types and will remain effective until further notice. The revised Mauritius charges follow previous surcharge announcements covering Asia–Africa services . CMA CGM noted that the new surcharges are separate from basic ocean freight rates. Bunker-related charges, terminal handling charges, safety and security fees and other applicable costs may also be added. For shipments originating in China, the carrier said the surcharges will be subject to the relevant filing requirements with the Shanghai Shipping Exchange or may be incorporated into the ocean freight rate. The Mediterranean and North Africa surcharge will also be implemented in accordance with applicable local filing and regulatory requirements. The announcements provide revised pricing conditions for cargo moving from major Asian export markets to Mediterranean and Indian Ocean destinations during the final weeks of 2026.

articles.title: Yang Ming reports strong Q3 profit amid higher freight rates
articles.summary: Yang Ming Marine Transport Corporation reported an after-tax net profit of NT$18.57 billion (US$584.75 million) for the third quarter of 2026, supported by stronger cargo demand, higher freight rates and continued capacity constraints across major shipping routes. The Taiwanese container shipping company generated...
articles.body: Yang Ming Marine Transport Corporation reported an after-tax net profit of NT$18.57 billion (US$584.75 million) for the third quarter of 2026, supported by stronger cargo demand, higher freight rates and continued capacity constraints across major shipping routes. The Taiwanese container shipping company generated consolidated quarterly revenue of NT$64.15 billion (US$2.02 billion), while earnings per share reached NT$5.32, according to financial results approved by its board on 10 November. For the first nine months of 2026, Yang Ming recorded consolidated revenue of NT$148.73 billion (US$4.68 billion), representing an 18% increase compared with the corresponding period of 2025. After-tax net profit reached NT$25.74 billion (US$810.56 million), with cumulative earnings per share of NT$7.37. Stronger demand and capacity constraints support earnings Yang Ming attributed its financial performance to improving demand across long-haul container shipping trades since the second quarter, with cargo volumes maintaining momentum throughout the traditional third-quarter peak season. Port congestion and the continued diversion of vessels around the Cape of Good Hope further restricted effective shipping capacity, contributing to higher average freight rates. The combination of stronger cargo volumes and improved freight rates supported the carrier’s revenue growth during the first nine months of the year. Fleet expansion expected to outpace demand in 2027 Looking ahead, Yang Ming cited projections from maritime consultancy Drewry indicating that global container shipping capacity will increase by 5% in 2026, compared with demand growth of 3.1%. For 2027, fleet capacity is projected to expand by 8.8%, while demand is expected to grow by 6.2%, suggesting that supply growth will continue to exceed cargo demand. The carrier expects relatively stable demand during the fourth quarter of 2026, with an earlier Lunar New Year potentially encouraging a pre-holiday increase in shipments. However, port congestion could create additional supply chain bottlenecks. Yang Ming identified geopolitical developments, US-China trade policies, port labour negotiations, terminal efficiency and bunker fuel price volatility as key factors influencing the container shipping market. The company also expects environmental regulations, including measures introduced by the European Union and the United Kingdom, to encourage slower vessel operating speeds and the gradual retirement of older ships, potentially reducing effective fleet capacity. Yang Ming strengthens Singapore operations Alongside its financial results, Yang Ming’s board authorised its wholly owned subsidiary, Yang Ming (Singapore) Pte. Ltd., to acquire office property in Singapore. The investment is intended to support the carrier’s long-term regional operations and strengthen its presence in one of Asia’s principal transshipment hubs. Yang Ming said it would continue monitoring cargo demand and trade flows while pursuing fleet and container renewal initiatives to improve operational efficiency and maintain its service network amid changing market conditions.

REUTERS/Hannibal Hanschke//File Photo By Holger Hansen BERLIN, Nov 11 (Reuters) – The German government will go ahead with a planned 24-terawatt-hour crisis gas reserve to be funded by user surcharges, the economy ministry said, following criticism over missed storage targets for the winter heating season this year. The state buffer, which amounts to about 10% of the nation’s gas storage capacity, will be accumulated over up to three years, the ministry said in a statement on Wednesday. It said the move would address severe disruptions, for example from acts of sabotage, and does not replace the private sector’s seasonal stock-keeping duties. “The gas reserve does not relieve market participants of their responsibilities, which include winter preparedness as well as meeting supply obligations,” it said. To fund the reserve, households would likely face 0.3% to 0.5% higher gas prices, the ministry said. Opposition parties and Italy have criticized Germany’s low gas storage levels , which stood at 62% at end-October, below a target of 70%. Berlin has said its supplies are still secure as it now has more purchasing options via liquefied natural gas terminals and through pipelines from Norway than it had in 2022 when Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine triggered an energy crisis. The government also plans a range of measures to tighten gas market regulation, including mandatory seasonal stock keeping for gas utilities, a ministry spokesperson told Reuters on Wednesday. A person close to the matter said the plans include closer monitoring of inventories by the network regulator, while the government is also considering measures to secure gas supplies to power plants and industrial sites. Documents seen by Reuters showed that setting up the reserve will likely cost between €1.26 billion ($1.41 billion) and €1.81 billion, plus running costs. REUTERS/Dado Ruvic/Illustration/File Photo By Ruth Liao and Stephen Stapczynski Nov 11, 2026 (Bloomberg) –Polish energy company Orlen SA terminated one of its long-term liquefied natural gas contracts with QatarEnergy, citing the export giant’s inability to deliver as the conflict in the Middle East disrupts shipments. The annulment is the first by a customer of QatarEnergy, which supplied about a fifth of the world’s LNG until the war between the US and Iran throttled its shipments through the Strait of Hormuz and damaged its export infrastructure. It is another blow for the emirate, as the nation’s budget deficit increases because of the lost revenue. Missile strikes in March damaged the world’s largest LNG export plant in Qatar — badly damaging two of its 14 production units and forcing the supplier to declare force majeure, a legal clause allowing producers to miss deliveries due to factors beyond their control, on shipments for the first time. Iranian attacks on vessels continue to slow shipping through Hormuz, cutting gas flows to a third of pre-war levels last month. The inability to meet contractual obligations led to the dissolving of the contract that was meant to run until 2034 and had an estimated value of €570 million ($637 million) this year, Orlen said in a statement on Tuesday. The agreement remains in force for a further 60 days. Orlen will retain a second supply contract with Qatar. Qatar sells most of its fuel under long-term contracts and has put its customers in Europe and Asia on force majeure notice for months. That’s forced buyers to replace the supply with spot cargoes, prices for which are at the highest level in years. Extended use of the clause eventually gives buyers the right to walk away, typically after a prolonged period of canceled deliveries. Qatar has been extending the measure every month, with its latest notice affecting shipments through the end of the year. Buyers are “unable to make longer term arrangements for alternative supply if their Qatari contract remains on foot, because if the volumes return at some point, it would leave the customer with an overly contracted position,” said Saul Kavonic, senior energy analyst at MST Marquee. “The longer the disruption lasts, the more customers will come under pressure to pursue this alternative.” Read More: Qatar Rewrites Its Gas Playbook With Old Tankers and New Tactics The canceled Qatari contract was Poland’s first LNG purchase agreement, paving the way for the European country to begin importing the super-chilled fuel in 2015. The contract was priced at 16% of Brent oil, according to a BloombergNEF database of LNG contracts, making it among the most expensive term deals in effect. Orlen’s second deal with Qatar is linked to natural gas benchmarks. Meanwhile, the Polish company has signed deals to procure LNG from projects in Texas and Louisiana including Port Arthur and Plaquemines — more affordable and flexible options that allows its trading desk to resell shipments. © 2026 Bloomberg L.P. November 11, 2026 Image courtesy Furetank Swedish tanker operator Furetank has been named a regional winner of the EY Entrepreneur Of The Year 2026 awards, receiving the Best International Growth distinction for combining fleet expansion, technological innovation and environmental performance. The award recognizes Furetank's long-term investment strategy, which has helped position the company as a leader in developing more environmentally efficient product tankers while maintaining profitable growth. Lars Höglund, who has led the company's development for nearly four decades, accepted the award during a ceremony at Hotel Elite Park Avenue in Gothenburg. The jury highlighted Höglund's commitment to technological innovation, employee involvement and sustainable development in one of the world's most capital-intensive industries. "For almost four decades, this entrepreneur has made bold, long-term investments in one of the world's riskiest and most capital-intensive industries," the jury stated, recognizing Furetank's emphasis on safety, workplace culture and continuous improvement. Furetank's growth has been closely tied to its VINGA vessel series, developed in cooperation with FKAB Marine Design. The company and its partners have ordered 26 tankers in the series, designed to reduce the environmental footprint of petroleum product transportation. The business has grown from a family operation with a single tanker in the 1950s to a shipping company employing approximately 300 people and generating annual revenue of SEK 1.5 billion. "It all goes back to a point ten years ago when we had to renew our fleet, just as society was turning its attention to the environment," Höglund said. "Together with FKAB Marine Design, we developed a vessel design that today gives us the ships with the smallest environmental footprint in their class globally." Höglund said the fleet investment demonstrated that improved environmental performance and commercial profitability can go hand in hand. articles.body: Balaena, Kongsberg Team Up to Bring Arctic Hunter USV to Royal Navy Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 11, 2026 (Credit: Baleana) British shipbuilding group Balaena and Norway's Kongsberg Maritime have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to advance the Arctic Hunter uncrewed surface vessel (USV), a proposed solution for the Royal Navy's emerging Type 92 anti-submarine warfare requirement. The agreement, signed at Kongsberg Maritime's offices in Norway on November 11, builds on an existing relationship between the companies and aims to combine British shipbuilding capabilities with Norwegian vessel design and autonomous technologies. Arctic Hunter is designed for uncrewed naval operations in extreme Arctic conditions, combining Kongsberg Maritime's commercial vessel designs and remote and autonomous technologies with sonar and military communications capabilities from UK defence technology company Thales. The proposed vessel is intended to provide persistent submarine detection capabilities in the High North, using a commercial shipbuilding approach designed to accelerate construction and delivery. Under the proposed program, the vessels would be built at Balaena's Birkenhead shipyard in the UK, with the ambition of delivering units ready for military integration before the end of the decade. The Birkenhead facility has four large dry docks, a non-tidal wet basin, fabrication facilities and a dedicated modular construction hall. Headquartered in Cornwall, Balaena employs more than 2,000 people and operates shipbuilding, repair and engineering facilities across the UK and Gibraltar, including 12 dry docks. The companies intend to use their collaboration to support the development of future naval capabilities and strengthen maritime security across the North Atlantic and High North.

articles.body: Physical AI in Shipbuilding: Fincantieri Partners with Poste Italiane, TIM Maritime Activity Reports, Inc. November 11, 2026 Copyright Casimiro/AdobeStock New industrial AI initiative targets shipyard automation, robotics and preservation of technical expertise across Fincantieri's global shipbuilding operations. Italian shipbuilding group Fincantieri has announced a strategic partnership with Poste Italiane and telecommunications company TIM to establish Italy's first integrated national Physical AI ecosystem, designed to accelerate the application of artificial intelligence, robotics and automation in shipbuilding. The initiative, called "Fincantieri Ontology," is a central component of the company's 2026–2030 industrial plan, F4 (Fast Forward Further Future), which prioritizes digitalization, automation and the protection of industrial knowledge. The partnership combines the three companies' technological capabilities to develop a secure digital infrastructure that integrates AI directly into ship design, construction and vessel management. Fincantieri Ontology will focus on automating shipyard design and production processes, while the parallel "Navis Sapiens" initiative targets the digitalization of ships themselves, ultimately supporting increasingly autonomous vessel operations. A key element involves creating digital representations of industrial processes, capturing technical expertise and using AI models to optimize manufacturing operations. The companies plan to develop four-dimensional design and construction models, enabling shipyard workers and robotic systems to receive AI-optimized work packages and daily production instructions. The initiative supports Fincantieri's industrial workload valued at approximately $81 billion (€70 billion), extending through 2036. Its supply chain includes 7,000 small and medium-sized enterprises, 18 shipyards worldwide and approximately 100,000 people accessing its facilities daily. Another objective is preserving accumulated shipbuilding knowledge while transitioning traditional manufacturing roles toward digitally enabled production. "Data and Artificial Intelligence are the driving forces behind our 2026–2030 Industrial Plan," said Pierroberto Folgiero, CEO and General Manager of Fincantieri. "With the launch of this strategic partnership, we are not simply digitalizing an industrial process; we are documenting and protecting the ontology of our technical culture." Fincantieri said the partnership will establish a protected computing environment combining local AI processing and secure cloud infrastructure, supporting cybersecurity and safeguarding sensitive industrial data while accelerating robotics adoption across its shipbuilding operations.

The company will work with the Royal Navy to develop Atlantic Net, a network of autonomous maritime systems, underwater sensors and artificial intelligence designed to monitor the North Atlantic and protect critical subsea infrastructure. Ocean Infinity will work with specialist partners to combine maritime platforms, underwater sensing, communications, remote operations, and data services into a persistent surveillance capability. The company operates a fleet of remotely operated and lean-crewed vessels used for offshore surveys and subsea operations. One of its Armada vessels participated in Royal Navy trials earlier this year. The initial programme will also draw on UK technology suppliers, with much of the equipment expected to come from small and medium-sized businesses. articles.body: Interconnectors November 11, 2026 · 1 minute ago Main construction starts on central part of interconnection between Western Isles and UK NS Nadja Skopljak Managing Editor 3 minutes read LinkedIn X Email SSEN Transmission SSEN Transmission has started main construction of the Lewis Hub project, a central part of the interconnector that will link the Scottish Western Isles to the UK national electricity transmission network for the first time. The groundbreaking, which marks the project’s progression from initial site preparation into main construction, was held on November 5 at the Lewis Hub site at Arnish Moor near Stornoway. Lewis Hub will comprise a high-voltage direct current (HVDC) converter station and AC substation and will form a central part of the wider Western Isles HVDC Link. The 1.8 GW interconnector will consist of approximately 83 kilometers of underground cable and 81 kilometers of subsea cable, connecting the Lewis Hub HVDC converter station and AC substation on the Isle of Lewis to the mainland. In the same week the groundbreaking took place, Highlands-based civil engineering contractor RJ McLeod signed a contract to deliver the first major package of construction works that will prepare the site for the HVDC converter station, AC substation and associated infrastructure. “Breaking ground on the Lewis Hub is a hugely significant moment for the project and for the Western Isles. A direct connection between the Western Isles and the main GB transmission network has been an ambition for decades. Through the Lewis Hub and wider Western Isles Connection, we are now turning that ambition into reality, unlocking the islands’ vast renewable energy potential and strengthening the electricity network for generations to come," said Sandy Mactaggart , Director of Offshore Delivery at SSEN Transmission. “But our ambition is about much more than delivering new infrastructure. We want this investment to create a lasting legacy for the islands, supporting local infrastructure, developing skills and creating opportunities for local businesses, while working with key partners to find mutually beneficial solutions that support long-term economic growth." The Western Isles HVDC Link is a key component of SSEN Transmission’s planned £22 billion investment program to upgrade the north of Scotland’s electricity transmission grid. The Scottish Government Marine Directorate at the beginning of 2026 granted the variation to the existing marine license , approved in 2021, for the subsea cable link, greenlighting the needed increase in capacity. Hitachi Energy is delivering the HVDC converter stations for the project and NKT the power cable system . "We are proud to support SSEN Transmission by delivering the complete 525 kV HVDC power cable system, covering design, production, installation and testing across the onshore and offshore sections," NKT said. "This is the scale of infrastructure needed to turn renewable energy potential into a more secure and interconnected power system. We are proud to be part of Western Isles and look forward to the milestones ahead." According to SSEN Transmission, the Lewis Hub project is expected to support more than 70 apprenticeship and trainee opportunities and is already delivering wider benefits to the local community, with a £1.06 million (approximately €1.27 million) Lewis Hub Local Fund due to launch soon. Together with future local funds associated with proposed transmission projects in the Western Isles, the fund is expected to contribute to more than £5 million in community benefit funding, subject to the relevant projects securing consent and progressing to main construction. The acquisition takes Monjasa’s owned fleet to 20 tankers, alongside around 10 ships on time charter. Group chief executive Anders Østergaard described the purchase as the company’s largest single tonnage acquisition, highlighting the benefits of taking on five identical vessels with established operating costs and technical requirements. “Finding five sister vessels of this quality, at competitive market terms and with an operating profile that fits our existing fleet, is not something you come across every day,” he said. The tankers will initially support Monjasa’s West African operations, although the company also sees opportunities to employ them in commercial freight trading and elsewhere in its global supply network.
